body.objective: Students will be able to learn intermediate techniques.
successCriteria: I can perform intermediate techniques with precision
I can maintain tools and equipment
body.hook: Anyone can follow a recipe or a cut list once. Intermediate skill means doing it consistently, with precision, and knowing what to do when something goes wrong. That's what separates a hobbyist from someone ready for the workplace.

study.title: Precision and Problem-Solving
study.question: How do skilled workers achieve consistent quality?
study.passage:
Choose the task for your CTS area:
• Foods: dice an onion into 0.5 cm cubes, then make a basic sauce (for example, a roux-based white sauce) with a smooth texture and no lumps.
• Construction: cut and join two pieces at a 90° angle within 1 mm tolerance using a square, a saw and wood glue.
• Computing: write a program that reads 10 numbers and finds their mean, then debug three planted errors.
• Design or fashion: sew a straight 1.5 cm seam allowance along 50 cm of fabric within 2 mm.
Step 1 (20 minutes): Complete the task three times. Measure or test each result against the standard.
Step 2 (10 minutes): Maintenance: clean and check your tools. Foods: sharpen or hone knives and sanitize surfaces. Construction: check blades and clear sawdust. Computing: organize files and comment code. Sewing: change dull needles and clean the bobbin area.
Step 3 (10 minutes): Troubleshoot using the "5 Whys": ask "Why did this happen?" up to five times to reach the root cause. Example: Sauce was lumpy → flour added too fast → I didn't whisk while adding → I was distracted → I had too many steps at once → Next time, prepare ingredients first (mise en place).
study.source: Original activity written for this lesson.

Complete it three times and measure each result
Troubleshoot a problem with the 5 Whys
discussion: How consistent were your three attempts?
What did measuring show that looking didn't?
What maintenance did your tools need?
What root cause did the 5 Whys reveal?
study.product: Write a short quality report on your three attempts: measurements, whether each met the tolerance, one problem you troubleshot with the 5 Whys and your plan for the next attempt.

examples.title: Tolerance
examples.problem: A board must be 300 mm ± 1 mm. Is 301.5 mm acceptable?

examples.title: Consistency
examples.problem: Your dice were 0.5, 0.8 and 0.4 cm. What does this show?
examples.answer: Inconsistent cuts; the technique needs work

examples.title: 5 Whys
examples.problem: Your program crashes. Use the first two whys.
steps: Why did it crash? Why did that happen?
examples.answer: It divided by zero → the list was empty because input wasn't read

examples.title: Maintenance
examples.problem: Why does a dull knife increase risk?
examples.answer: It needs more force and can slip

practice.q: Why measure instead of judging by eye?
practice.a: Measurements are objective and reveal small errors.

practice.q: Why does consistency matter in a workplace?
practice.a: Customers and employers expect the same quality every time.

practice.q: Why fix the root cause instead of the symptom?
practice.a: Otherwise the problem keeps coming back.

practice.q: How does tool maintenance improve safety?
practice.a: Well-maintained tools behave predictably and need less force.

misconceptions: Fixing symptoms instead of root causes
